items.stem:
Read the following extract from a short story set in Cairo, Egypt.

Every evening Karim's uncle climbed to the roof to fly his pigeons. He whistled, waved a long stick with a rag tied to it, and the flock rose over the satellite dishes and the washing lines.
"Why do they always come back?" Karim asked.
His uncle shrugged. "Because this is where they are fed. Freedom is a big sky, ya Karim. But it is not dinner."
That autumn, when Karim's visa letter came, he climbed to the roof alone and stood a long time, watching the birds circle and return, circle and return.

Identify the moment of epiphany in this extract and explain its significance.
items.answer: Epiphany: on receiving his visa letter, Karim understands his uncle's words – he too will need to balance freedom with the pull of home.
items.markingKey: Epiphany: on receiving his visa letter, Karim understands his uncle's words – he too will need to balance freedom with the pull of home. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

Read the following extract from a coming-of-age novel in which the narrator attends her brother's trial.

The courtroom was smaller than the ones on television, and quieter. Nobody shouted "Objection!".
Danny sat in a suit that belonged to our uncle. The sleeves covered his hands. He looked about nine.
When the lawyer called him "the defendant", I wanted to stand up and say his name. His name is Danny. He is scared of moths. He taught me to ride a bike.
I didn't stand up. That was the day I learned that justice is a room where you are not allowed to speak.

Explain how the closing generalisation "That was the day I learned" contributes to the meaning of the text.
items.answer: The closing generalisation "That was the day I learned": the specific scene becomes a turning point in her understanding of the adult world.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a short story set in Kyoto, Japan, which keeps some Japanese words, as many translations do.

On the last night of Obon, Grandmother gave Haruto a paper lantern and a pen. "Write his name," she said.
Haruto wrote OJIICHAN in careful letters, because he could not remember his grandfather's face, only the smell of his pipe.
At the river the lanterns drifted away in hundreds, each one a small, swaying light. Haruto watched his until he could not tell it from the others.
"Now he knows the way back," Grandmother said. "And we know the way to let go."

Explain how one detail in the extract connects to a wider theme.
items.answer: Theme: grief, memory and tradition. How it is developed: Retained terms like "Obon" and "OJIICHAN" situate the story in Japanese culture and its ancestor rituals. Haruto's memory survives only as "the smell of his pipe", showing faint but precious grief. The lanterns symbolise spirits; as Haruto loses sight of his among hundreds, private grief merges into shared tradition. Grandmother's parallel final lines provide an epiphany: the ritual teaches the living "the way to let go".
items.markingKey: Theme: grief, memory and tradition. How it is developed: Retained terms like "Obon" and "OJIICHAN" situate the story in Japanese culture and its ancestor rituals. Haruto's memory survives only as "the smell of his pipe", showing faint but precious grief. The lanterns symbolise spirits; as Haruto loses sight of his among hundreds, private grief merges into shared tradition. Grandmother's parallel final lines provide an epiphany: the ritual teaches the living "the way to let go". Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a short story set in Valparaíso, Chile.

For twenty years my father kept the key in his wallet, behind his London bus pass. A small brass key to a blue door on Cerro Alegre.
"Why keep it?" I asked once. "The house is probably gone."
He didn't answer.
When we finally went back, the door was green. A café now. My father stood outside for a long time, then took out the key, kissed it and slipped it into the café's tip jar.
"There," he said, in Spanish. "Now it is home again."

Explain how "He didn't answer." reflects the cultural setting of the story.
items.answer: Silence: "He didn't answer." – the one-line paragraph suggests feelings too deep or painful to express.
items.markingKey: Silence: "He didn't answer." – the one-line paragraph suggests feelings too deep or painful to express. items.stem:
Read the following opening of a dystopian short story.

The last tree in the city stood in a glass case in Victory Square, guarded by two soldiers and a sign: DO NOT BREATHE ON THE EXHIBIT.
Children came on school trips to look at it. They were told it had been saved by the Council, who had also, the teachers explained, saved everyone from the dangerous old days when trees grew wherever they liked.
Nadia, aged twelve, pressed her nose to the glass and saw something no one else had noticed.
A new leaf.

How does one image in this extract carry meaning beyond its literal sense?
items.answer: Theme: nature, control and hope. How it is developed: The tree in a "glass case" guarded by soldiers, with the absurd sign "DO NOT BREATHE ON THE EXHIBIT", shows how rare and controlled nature has become. Irony in the teachers' claim that the Council saved everyone from "the dangerous old days" exposes propaganda that rewrites history. Nadia's discovery of "A new leaf", isolated in a one-line paragraph, symbolises hope and suggests resistance can grow, with a pun on turning over a new leaf.
items.markingKey: Theme: nature, control and hope. How it is developed: The tree in a "glass case" guarded by soldiers, with the absurd sign "DO NOT BREATHE ON THE EXHIBIT", shows how rare and controlled nature has become. Irony in the teachers' claim that the Council saved everyone from "the dangerous old days" exposes propaganda that rewrites history. Nadia's discovery of "A new leaf", isolated in a one-line paragraph, symbolises hope and suggests resistance can grow, with a pun on turning over a new leaf. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem:
Text A: poem about leaving home, from a contemporary anthology.

Departure Lounge

My mother packed the spices first –
cardamom, turmeric, a jar of chilli
wrapped in a jumper like a sleeping child –
as if a country could be carried
in small glass jars.

At the gate, she did not look back.
I did. I am still
looking.

Text B: letter written in 1962 by a young woman who had recently emigrated, to her sister.

Dear Nalini,
The flat is small and the radiator knocks all night like a neighbour who wants to come in. At the factory they call me "Nelly" because they cannot say my name. I let them.
I have found a shop that sells cardamom, but it tastes of the box it came in.
Do not tell Amma I cry on the bus. Tell her I have a warm coat and that the English are polite. Both are true.
Your loving sister,
Saroja

Compare how the two texts present the experience of leaving home.
items.answer: Both texts use spices and small domestic details to represent home and loss. In the poem, spices are "wrapped in a jumper like a sleeping child", and the conceit "as if a country could be carried / in small glass jars" shows the impossibility of carrying home. In the letter, cardamom "tastes of the box it came in", showing home cannot be recreated. The poem uses free verse, enjambement and a lingering final word ("looking") to show grief continuing into the present; the letter uses intimate address, understated sentences ("I let them.") and selective truth to protect her mother. The poem looks back years later; the letter is written in the raw present of arrival.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Both texts use spices and small domestic details to represent home and loss. In the poem, spices are "wrapped in a jumper like a sleeping child", and the conceit "as if a country could be carried / in small glass jars" shows the impossibility of carrying home. In the letter, cardamom "tastes of the box it came in", showing home cannot be recreated. The poem uses free verse, enjambement and a lingering final word ("looking") to show grief continuing into the present; the letter uses intimate address, understated sentences ("I let them.") and selective truth to protect her mother. The poem looks back years later; the letter is written in the raw present of arrival. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling. Comparison must be sustained across both texts (criterion B).

Read the following extract from a short story set in Cape Town.

The poster had been on the lamppost for three weeks: MISSING – BRUNO – REWARD. The rain had washed the dog's face into a grey smudge.
Thabo passed it every morning. Every morning he told himself it wasn't his business.
Then, on Thursday, behind the fish shop, something whined.
It was thin, and it was muddy, and one ear stood up like a question mark.
Thabo crouched. The dog looked at him. He looked at the poster. He looked at the reward. He thought about his mother's empty purse.
"Come on, Bruno," he whispered. "Let's get you home."

Explain how the ambiguous ending contributes to the meaning of the text.
items.answer: The ambiguous ending: we do not learn whether Thabo takes the reward; his gentle words suggest kindness comes first, leaving the reader to judge his motives.
items.markingKey: The ambiguous ending: we do not learn whether Thabo takes the reward; his gentle words suggest kindness comes first, leaving the reader to judge his motives. items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel that follows its main character from childhood to adolescence.

At eleven, Ama would not go past the jetty. The lake was too dark, and her grandmother had told her about the river spirit who collected disobedient children.
At fourteen, she swam to the jetty and back every evening, counting strokes to keep the fear quiet.
At sixteen, the summer her grandmother died, Ama swam out past the last buoy, turned on her back and floated, looking up at a sky that seemed, for the first time, to belong to her.
She did not count.

How does one image in this extract carry meaning beyond its literal sense?
items.answer: Theme: growing up as overcoming fear and claiming independence. How it is developed: The structure – "At eleven ... At fourteen ... At sixteen" – compresses Ama's growth into three stages. At first she obeys her grandmother's story about the river spirit; then she controls her fear by "counting strokes"; finally, after her grandmother's death, she swims "past the last buoy", symbolically leaving childhood limits behind. The sky that "seemed ... to belong to her" and the one-line ending "She did not count." show her new freedom.
items.markingKey: Theme: growing up as overcoming fear and claiming independence. How it is developed: The structure – "At eleven ... At fourteen ... items.markingKey: Foreignisation keeps the source culture visible (retaining words and customs); domestication adapts the text to feel familiar to the target audience. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Every object in a story is a symbol." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Symbols are emphasised, repeated or placed at key moments; ordinary details are not automatically symbolic.
items.markingKey: Symbols are emphasised, repeated or placed at key moments; ordinary details are not automatically symbolic. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Every short story needs a dramatic climax." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Many short stories build to a quiet epiphany or small gesture rather than a dramatic event.
items.markingKey: Many short stories build to a quiet epiphany or small gesture rather than a dramatic event. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a short story set in Cairo, Egypt.

Every evening Karim's uncle climbed to the roof to fly his pigeons. He whistled, waved a long stick with a rag tied to it, and the flock rose over the satellite dishes and the washing lines.
"Why do they always come back?" Karim asked.
His uncle shrugged. "Because this is where they are fed. Freedom is a big sky, ya Karim. But it is not dinner."
That autumn, when Karim's visa letter came, he climbed to the roof alone and stood a long time, watching the birds circle and return, circle and return.

What message or theme does the writer explore here? Support your answer with evidence.
items.answer: Theme: freedom, home and migration. How it is developed: The pigeons rising "over the satellite dishes and the washing lines" suggest escape from crowded daily life, yet they always return. The uncle's aphorism "Freedom is a big sky ... But it is not dinner" makes them symbols of the tension between freedom and belonging. When Karim receives his visa letter, he watches them "circle and return, circle and return", and the repetition shows him seeing his own dilemma in their flight.
items.markingKey: Theme: freedom, home and migration. How it is developed: The pigeons rising "over the satellite dishes and the washing lines" suggest escape from crowded daily life, yet they always return. The uncle's aphorism "Freedom is a big sky ... But it is not dinner" makes them symbols of the tension between freedom and belonging. When Karim receives his visa letter, he watches them "circle and return, circle and return", and the repetition shows him seeing his own dilemma in their flight. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel that follows its main character from childhood to adolescence.

At eleven, Ama would not go past the jetty. The lake was too dark, and her grandmother had told her about the river spirit who collected disobedient children.
At fourteen, she swam to the jetty and back every evening, counting strokes to keep the fear quiet.
At sixteen, the summer her grandmother died, Ama swam out past the last buoy, turned on her back and floated, looking up at a sky that seemed, for the first time, to belong to her.
She did not count.

Explain how the central symbol of this extract connects to its theme of growing up as overcoming fear and claiming independence.
items.answer: Theme: growing up as overcoming fear and claiming independence. How it is developed: The structure – "At eleven ... At fourteen ... At sixteen" – compresses Ama's growth into three stages. At first she obeys her grandmother's story about the river spirit; then she controls her fear by "counting strokes"; finally, after her grandmother's death, she swims "past the last buoy", symbolically leaving childhood limits behind. The sky that "seemed ... to belong to her" and the one-line ending "She did not count." show her new freedom.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a short story set in Kyoto, Japan, which keeps some Japanese words, as many translations do.

On the last night of Obon, Grandmother gave Haruto a paper lantern and a pen. "Write his name," she said.
Haruto wrote OJIICHAN in careful letters, because he could not remember his grandfather's face, only the smell of his pipe.
At the river the lanterns drifted away in hundreds, each one a small, swaying light. Haruto watched his until he could not tell it from the others.
"Now he knows the way back," Grandmother said. "And we know the way to let go."

How does ending on Grandmother's words shape the reader's experience of the text?
items.answer: Ending on Grandmother's words: the final line provides the story's epiphany and turns description into meaning.
items.markingKey: Ending on Grandmother's words: the final line provides the story's epiphany and turns description into meaning. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a short story set in Valparaíso, Chile.

For twenty years my father kept the key in his wallet, behind his London bus pass. A small brass key to a blue door on Cerro Alegre.
"Why keep it?" I asked once. "The house is probably gone."
He didn't answer.
When we finally went back, the door was green. A café now. My father stood outside for a long time, then took out the key, kissed it and slipped it into the café's tip jar.
"There," he said, in Spanish. "Now it is home again."

What message or theme does the writer explore here? Support your answer with evidence.
items.answer: Theme: exile, memory and letting go. How it is developed: The "small brass key" kept "behind his London bus pass" juxtaposes the father's two lives and symbolises exile and hope of return. His silence when asked why he keeps it shows emotion too deep to express. The fragments "the door was green. A café now." reveal the past has been replaced, yet he kisses the key and gives it to the café: an epiphany in which home is honoured by letting go. "Now it is home again" redefines home as a relationship, not a building.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Symbols are more effective when readers have to work out their meaning."
items.answer: Symbols work best when they are suggestive but grounded in clear textual emphasis.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: active interpretation engages readers; subtlety rewards rereading. Arguments against: obscure symbols may be missed; some clarity helps all readers. Supported judgement: Symbols work best when they are suggestive but grounded in clear textual emphasis.

items.stem: "An epiphany is the most important element of a short story." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Epiphanies often give stories their meaning, but they depend on setting and conflict, and some stories deliberately withhold them.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it gives the story meaning; it is memorable. Arguments against: setting and conflict create the epiphany; some stories deliberately avoid resolution. Supported judgement: Epiphanies often give stories their meaning, but they depend on setting and conflict, and some stories deliberately withhold them. items.stem: "Translated literature can never be fully understood by readers from another culture." Discuss.
items.answer: Some nuance is always lost, but translated literature still communicates powerfully, especially when readers learn about its context.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: cultural references and wordplay are lost; context is unfamiliar. Arguments against: universal emotions cross cultures; translators and notes bridge gaps. Supported judgement: Some nuance is always lost, but translated literature still communicates powerfully, especially when readers learn about its context.
